meta.title: Onmal — your teammates' words, in your language
meta.desc: Understands your teammates' foreign language during games and shows it as subtitles over your screen, in your language. A free real-time interpreter that runs on your own PC.
privacy.meta.title: Privacy policy — Onmal
privacy.meta.desc: Onmal has no servers. Everything is processed inside your own PC, and with the default settings no data leaves it.
terms.meta.title: Terms of use — Onmal
terms.meta.desc: The conditions and limits for using Onmal. Use it only in conversations you are part of.
hero.lede: Missing calls because you can't tell what a foreign teammate just said. Onmal listens for you and puts translated subtitles right over your game.
hero.note: The microphone stays shut unless you turn it on yourself. Your teammates' voices are processed inside your PC, and conversations are never sent anywhere.
hero.version_note: The core works end to end. This is before alpha, so expect rough edges.
how.h2: Subtitles appear before the sentence even ends.
how.lede: Four stages run back-to-back inside your PC. No server round-trips means no extra delay — and it keeps working if your internet drops.
how.t1: Only the app your team talks through
how.p1: In-game voice chat or Discord — Windows per-process capture takes audio only from the app you choose. Other apps' sounds stay out.
how.p2: Voice detection cuts out only the parts where someone is talking. Gunfire and music are filtered out; when it's quiet, nothing happens.
how.t3: Detects the language on its own
how.p3: No need to pick a language in advance. Russian or Portuguese — it detects and transcribes.
how.t4: In your language, over the game
how.p4: Click-through subtitles in a spot that doesn't cover the action. Your controls are never blocked.
shots.h2: This is what you get after installing.
shots.lede: Not mock-ups — these are screenshots of the app itself. There are only three screens: pick on Home, adjust in Settings, check in Info.
shots.c1: Home — where the sound comes from, and your language. That is all you set.
shots.c2: Settings — subtitle size and position, window colour, app language. Light and dark both included.
shots.c3: Info — how to use it, the hotkeys, and the legal documents. Readable without internet.
glossary.h2: Game words come out as game words.
glossary.lede: A translator has never heard a callout. When a word that exists only inside a game meets ordinary translation, its meaning disappears entirely. Onmal corrects those words first, then translates.
glossary.p1: Recognition hears the callout as a similar-sounding everyday word, and "two enemies are heading for B site" comes out as non-net. Nobody on your team can guess what that meant.
glossary.p2: The same sentence becomes Two enemies headed for B site. — because the misheard callout is put back to "B site" before anything is translated.
glossary.how: The correction is not a model but a fixed string replacement. Only words on the list change; anything else is left alone. There is no room for the translation to wander.
glossary.pack_common: Common — site, position, situation: words that belong to no single game
glossary.more: 266 entries in all, and 190 more alternate spellings of the same words — "B site" and "Bsite" point to the same place. Inside the app you can switch packs on and off, look at what is in them, and add the words you use yourself.
glossary.limit: For now this covers Korean ↔ English only. There are no glossaries for other language pairs yet.
audio.h2: It takes only the sound it needs.
audio.lede: It does not swallow everything your PC plays and filter afterwards. Point it at the one app your teammates' voices come out of, and only that app's audio arrives.
audio.t1: One app, and only that one
audio.p1: Windows can hand over the audio of a single process. Pick Discord and you get Discord — and if that app spawns a separate window of its own that makes sound, that comes along too.
audio.p2: [Check for sound] grabs whatever you picked for three seconds and measures one thing: whether sound is arriving. It records nothing, and it never looks at what was said.
audio.p3: While subtitles are being read aloud, your teammates' own voices can keep flowing to your speakers so nothing is cut off. Off by default.
audio.tts: Onmal can also read the subtitles out loud. It is there for the moments you cannot look at the screen, and it uses the voices installed in Windows — on a PC with no voice for that language, nothing is spoken. Off by default.
audio.novc: It never tells you to install a virtual audio cable. You only choose among playback devices already on your PC. Installing a new sound device is a nuisance to undo, and getting it wrong can silence your game entirely.
audio.limit: In-game voice chat comes out of the same app as the game itself. Choose that and gunfire and footsteps arrive with it, which makes recognition worse. A separate app like Discord is the cleanest. Which one works for you is best answered with [Check for sound] — it differs from game to game.
hands.h2: You never take your hands off the game.
hands.lede: Mid-fight there is no time to hunt for a window. Everything you reach for often is a single key.
hands.k7: Your line in your team's language, on the clipboard
hands.send: Alt+M goes as far as the clipboard. You paste it yourself — Onmal never types into the game window for you. The microphone opens only at that moment and closes as soon as the sentence ends; if you say nothing, it closes itself after 15 seconds.
hands.once: It is one press, one sentence — not hold-to-talk. Knowing when a key was released would mean watching every keystroke on the system, and that is the kind of thing anti-cheat objects to, so we do not do it.
name.p1: Onmal (온말) is pure Korean: on means whole or all — as in the whole world, all day long — and mal means words. Carrying a teammate's words across whole, whatever the language: that is what the app tries to do, and the name is that promise.
care.h2: Turn it on once, and it just works.
care.p1: Pick the app to listen to and your language — that's it. Installed games are found for you, and if you pick a game, subtitles start automatically the moment it launches.
care.t2: Bring your own API key if you want
care.p2: The built-in translation is free. If you want higher quality, you can plug in your own API key. Keys are stored encrypted on this computer only.
care.p3: Audio is processed in memory and discarded immediately. Subtitle history is off by default, and even switched on it stays on this computer. By default there is no recording, no uploading, and no account.
limits.h2: We also list what it can't do.
limits.lede: Better to know now than after installing.
limits.p1: Run the game in borderless or windowed mode for subtitles to appear on top. Most games have this in their display settings.
limits.p2: Capturing only one chosen app's audio works on Windows 11 (or Windows 10 build 20348+). Below that, all system audio is captured.
limits.p3: Even humans can't make out speech buried in gunfire and shouting. Neither can Onmal. When it fails, it says so instead of guessing.
limits.p4: No code is injected into game processes — nothing an anti-cheat would object to. The window-mode requirement above is the trade-off.
limits.t5: It does not translate on-screen text
limits.p5: Onmal handles sound and nothing else. There is no feature that reads the words printed in a game's UI or chat box, and none is planned.
limits.t6: It does not type into the game for you
limits.p6: A line translated with Alt+M goes as far as the clipboard. You are the one who pastes it into chat — Onmal never generates keystrokes into a game.
spec.h2:
It has to run alongside your game,
so we wrote these honestly.
spec.cpu_min: 4 cores · AVX2 (Intel 6th gen / Ryzen 1000 or newer)
spec.gfx_min: DirectX 11 (only to draw the subtitles) — recognition and translation run without a GPU
spec.gfx_rec: Dedicated GPU with Vulkan support · 8 GB VRAM or more
spec.note: The delays above are stage-by-stage measurements (speech detection, recognition, translation) with headroom added, taken on an NVIDIA RTX 4060. The whole path — from the moment a teammate speaks to the moment text appears on screen — has not been measured as one number yet, and neither has anything with a game running; both are planned for alpha and beta. AMD and Intel GPUs use the same Vulkan path but have not been measured. The default recognition and translation models ship inside the Steam install, so it works without an internet connection, and accuracy is chosen automatically to fit your GPU memory. This table carries the same values as the system requirements on the Steam store page.
lang.h2:
Every language Steam supports,
for everyone on Steam.
lang.lede: Three separate things, kept apart: what gets translated, what gets understood, and what is written on screen. Their ranges are not the same.
lang.p1: This is the one language pair that has actually been tested. Both directions ship inside the Steam install, so there is nothing to download. More pairs come with updates — but a pair is only called "supported" once it has been tested.
lang.p2: Speech recognition reaches far more languages than translation does. Even where no translation pair exists yet, what was said still appears as a subtitle in the original language — better than nothing at all.
lang.p3: This is the text in the app window and on this page, in all 31 languages Steam supports. 29 of them are AI translations, and the app says so plainly where you can see it.
maker.lede: Onmal is a free tool built by a single independent developer. No company, no investors, no server bills — which is exactly why free and unlimited can last.
maker.p1: With no servers there is nothing to pay every month, and so there is no reason to put a price or a usage cap on the app itself. There is no plan to add one.
maker.p2: What you get instead is one person's pace. Updates and replies come steadily, but not quickly. Bug reports and suggestions are always welcome — send them through Contact · bug reports below.
road.h2: From 0.1 to 1.0 — completion criteria, not dates.
road.lede: Each stage moves on only when its exit criteria are met, not when a calendar says so. No rushing — and the base app stays free the whole way.
road.vision: The end picture is a companion you leave on whenever you game, as naturally as a voice chat app. Install it, forget it — the moment a foreign call comes in, Onmal quietly goes to work. It is not trying to become a new platform: the focus stays on making translation excellent, with social layered lightly on top of the Steam and Discord you already use.
road.r1: The skeleton of real-time translated subtitles — local recognition, translation, overlay
road.r2: Stabilization — long sessions, running alongside real games
road.r3: Alpha test — a few testers go from install to subtitles with no instructions
road.r4: More translation — major language pairs bundled, OBS compatibility check
road.r6: Beta — Steam Playtest, speaker labels, per-game profiles
road.r7: Performance — low-end PCs and integrated graphics
road.r8: Release prep — store page, document review
road.r9: Release candidate — feature freeze, bug fixes only
road.r10: Full release — the always-on comfort of a voice app, still free
road.ea: It goes onto Steam as Early Access: released unfinished, and shaped together with the people using it. There is no release date — it goes up once the criteria above are met.
faq.h2: The questions we hear most before install.
faq.a1: Yes. The base app is free now and stays free after full release. No usage caps, no subscription, no account, no ads.
faq.a2: Onmal injects no code into game processes — to the game, it is just a separate window floating over the screen. The final call belongs to each game publisher though, so check the rules first in sensitive settings like tournaments.
faq.q3: Which games does it work with?
faq.a3: It is not tied to any specific game. If the game can run in borderless windowed mode, subtitles can appear on top. For audio, pick whichever app your team voice comes from — in-game voice chat or Discord.
faq.q4: Do I need an internet connection?
faq.a4: No. The default recognition and translation models ship inside the Steam install, so it works offline from the start. Only if you pick a more accurate recognition model yourself does that file get downloaded.
faq.q5: Does it translate my voice too?
faq.a5: Not by default. Onmal does not touch your microphone unless you turn it on — it listens to your teammates' voices, the sound playing on your PC, and shows subtitles only on your screen. If you do turn on sending your own lines in your teammates' language in Settings, one sentence at a time is translated into their language and placed on your clipboard. The microphone opens only for that moment, and you are the one who pastes it into the game chat.
faq.q6: Won't it slow down my game?
faq.a6: The game comes first — that is the design principle. It computes only while someone is speaking, picks the recognition model to fit your spare GPU memory, and ships with the heavy features off. Every PC differs though, so we will measure it alongside real games in alpha and beta and publish the numbers.
legal.h2: These documents are all that applies.
legal.lede: Onmal has no servers and no accounts, so the paperwork is short. The same documents are available inside the app. They are written in Korean, which is the authoritative text.
legal.p1: What is processed, and what is never collected. One-line summary: Onmal has no servers.
legal.p2: Conditions and restrictions — especially "only use it in conversations you are part of".
legal.p3: The copyright holders and licenses of the software, models and fonts Onmal uses — including what we deliberately chose not to use.

lic.meta.title: Copyright & licenses — Onmal
lic.meta.desc: The open-source software, models and fonts Onmal is built on, with each copyright holder and license — and the things we deliberately chose not to use.
lic.lede: Onmal runs on the software and models listed below. We name every copyright holder and license — and we also list what we deliberately chose not to use.
lic.same_in_app: The same notices ship inside the app (Info → Copyright & licenses), so they can be read without an internet connection.
lic.attr_p1: Onmal's local translation uses Opus-MT model weights from the Language Technology Research Group at the University of Helsinki (Helsinki-NLP). We converted them to ONNX format for inference; the weights themselves are unmodified.
lic.attr_p2: Licensing differs per language pair. The four pairs below are CC-BY-4.0 and therefore require attribution; the remaining pairs are Apache-2.0. Verified 2026-07-29.
lic.attr_apache: Apache-2.0 pairs: opus-mt-ko-en, opus-mt-ja-en, opus-mt-en-jap, opus-mt-en-zh, opus-mt-en-ru, opus-mt-es-en, opus-mt-en-es, opus-mt-roa-en, opus-mt-fr-en, opus-mt-en-fr, opus-mt-de-en.
lic.sw_note: FluentAssertions moved to a commercial license from 7.0 onward. Onmal pins 6.12.2, which is Apache-2.0.
lic.model_whisper: Speech recognition and language detection (ggml conversion)
lic.model_note: Model weights are not bundled with the app. They are downloaded separately, and each file is verified with SHA-256.
lic.icon_lucide: In use — 17 settings-window icons inlined as SVG paths. No package, no icon font.
lic.icon_note: ISC requires the copyright notice to be preserved. This table and the header comment in the app source are that notice.
lic.excl_h2: What we chose not to use
lic.excl_intro: We record what we rejected too. It saves us from re-litigating "why didn't we use that?" later, and it shows how Onmal handles licensing.
lic.excl_nllb: Non-commercial only. Regardless of translation quality, it does not go into this codebase.
lic.excl_parakeet: Fast, but it adds another attribution obligation. v1 ships with Whisper (MIT) alone.
lic.excl_ffmpeg: May not be compatible with the Steamworks SDK. We implemented resampling ourselves.
lic.excl_apple: Licensed only for software running on Apple operating systems. It cannot be used in a Windows app.
lic.excl_ct2: The license is fine, but there is no stable C API, so we would have to ship our own native wrapper. Replaced by ONNX Runtime.
lic.tm_p: Steam and the Steam logo are trademarks of Valve Corporation. Discord is a trademark of Discord Inc. Windows is a trademark of Microsoft Corporation. Onmal is not affiliated with these companies and uses the names only to describe compatibility.
lic.full_p: The complete text of each license is available here.
